series: Things Living In Your House, Part 6
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension, Jumping spiders: hunt during the day; often seen on windows and walls where insect prey gathers; https://extension.okstate.edu/programs/digital-diagnostics/insects-and-arthropods/jumping-spiders

Utah State University Extension, Jumping Spiders: most visible near windows and bright spots; not known to pose a health hazard; beneficial; catch in a jar and release outside; https://extension.usu.edu/planthealth/ipm/notes_nuisance/jumping-spiders.php

Australian Museum, Jumping spiders (Salticidae): daylight hunters with large eyes and excellent vision, used to track, stalk and judge distance before leaping; hunt by stalking, not webs; body 3-12 mm; males use colourful courtship displays; peacock spiders raise a coloured abdominal flap; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/spiders/jumping-spiders/

Wikipedia, Jumping spider (citing Land 1969, Foelix): largest spider family, over 6,000 described species; eight eyes, large front pair for 3D vision and range-finding; attaches a silk dragline before a jump and climbs back up it if it falls; legs straightened by a fast rise in blood pressure (hydraulics) rather than extensor muscles; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumping_spider

title: The Spider on Your Window Is Watching You Back
tiktok_caption: the spider on my window turned and looked at me 👀 it hunts with no web and jumps with blood pressure. Would you let it stay? 🏠 stay / 🫙 jar it outside

beats.say: The spider on your window can see you. And it just turned to look.
The jumping spider. Eight eyes, and two giant ones in front.
Outside, it hunts in daylight. No web at all.
It stalks a fly, judges the distance with those big eyes,
and jumps. Before it leaps, it glues down a silk safety line.
